landmarks.name: Boma National Park
landmarks.writeup: One of the largest national parks in Africa, known for its diverse wildlife and seasonal migration of antelopes.

wiki.extract: Boma National Park is a protected area in eastern South Sudan near the Ethiopian border. It was established in 1977 and covers 22,800 km2 (8,800 sq mi) of grasslands and floodplains.

landmarks.name: Nimule National Park
landmarks.writeup: Located near the border with Uganda, it features savannah landscapes and a variety of wildlife including elephants and lions.

wiki.extract: The Nimule National Park is a national park in South Sudan. It was established in 1954, and extends over an area of 410 km2, along the border with Uganda.

landmarks.name: Juba Nile Bridge
landmarks.writeup: A key infrastructure landmark in the capital city, connecting different parts of Juba across the White Nile.

wiki.extract: Juba is the capital and largest city of South Sudan. The city is situated on the White Nile and also serves as the capital of the Central Equatoria State. It is the most recently declared national capital and had a population of 525,953 in 2017. It has an area of 52 km2 (20 sq mi), with the metropolitan area covering 336 km2 (130 sq mi).

cultural_events.name: South Sudan Independence Day
cultural_events.writeup: Celebrated on July 9th, marking the country's independence from Sudan in 2011.

wiki.extract: South Sudan, officially the Republic of South Sudan, is a landlocked country in East Africa. It is bordered by Sudan to the north, Ethiopia to the east, Kenya to the southeast, Uganda to the south, the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the southwest, and the Central African Republic to the west. South Sudan's diverse landscape includes vast plains and plateaus, dry and tropical savannahs, inland floodplains, and forested mountains. The Nile River system is the defining physical feature of the country, running south to north across its center, which is dominated by a large swamp known as the Sudd. South Sudan has an estimated population of just over 12.7 million in 2024. Juba is the capital and largest city.

cultural_events.name: Traditional Dance Festivals
cultural_events.writeup: Various ethnic groups celebrate with traditional dances and music, showcasing their cultural heritage.

wiki.extract: A folk dance is a dance that reflects the life of the people of a certain country or region. Not all ethnic dances are folk dances. For example, ritual dances or dances of ritual origin are not considered to be folk dances. Ritual dances are usually called "religious dances" because of their purpose.

food_writeup: South Sudanese cuisine features staples like sorghum, millet, and maize, often served with stews made from meat, fish, and vegetables. Popular dishes include kisra (a type of bread) and asida (a porridge).
brief_history: South Sudan gained independence from Sudan in 2011 after decades of civil war. It is the world's youngest country but has faced ongoing internal conflicts and challenges in nation-building.

commentary.inflation_management: South Sudan has experienced one of the world's worst inflation episodes: 346.1% in 2016, the series high, and 213.0% in 2017, as the civil war destroyed oil revenues and the government printed money to fund the military. The pound collapsed and dollarization spread. A 2018 peace deal and tighter policy brought brief relief (-3.2% in 2022, the series low), but the 2023 Sudan war's pipeline damage reignited the crisis: 99.8% in 2024 and 97.6% projected for 2025. The central bank has no effective framework; monetary policy is fiscal policy, and fiscal policy is war finance.
commentary.debt_management: South Sudan's debt was born with the state and exploded with the war. From zero at independence in 2011, oil-backed borrowing and central bank advances drove it to 128.9% of GDP by 2016, the series high, as oil revenues collapsed and the pound imploded. It has fluctuated wildly since on the denominator (oil and the exchange rate) rather than policy: 62.5% projected for 2025. Much of the debt is oil-collateralized advances and arrears; transparency is minimal. Sustainability is hostage to a single pipeline through Sudan, which the 2023 Sudanese war damaged, cutting off the revenues that service the debt.

key_events.event: Independence (July 2011); GDP in USD terms peaked at $17.3bn on oil.
Oil shutdown in dispute with Sudan; revenues collapsed.
Civil war erupted (December 2013); hyperinflation began; debt exploded.
Peace deal signed; unity government formed (2020); inflation briefly turned negative.
Sudan's civil war (from April 2023) damaged the oil pipeline; revenues collapsed; inflation returned near 100%.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: The outlook is bleak and highly uncertain: South Sudan's economy is a hostage of two wars, its own and Sudan's. The base case is continued hyperinflation-risk, oil dependence, and humanitarian crisis. Upside requires peace in both countries and pipeline repair; downside is state collapse. This is less a forecast than a description of fragility: the numbers from 2024-25 (inflation near 100%, GDP under $6bn) describe an economy in free fall.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections. Note: the IMF data series for South Sudan begins in 2011.
